title: Microscopy
content:
# Microscopy

## Learning Objectives
By the end of this lesson, you should be able to:
- Describe the main types of microscopes and their uses
- Explain the difference between magnification and resolution
- Use a light microscope to observe cells
- Calculate magnification using the formula

## Introduction

Most cells are too small to see with the naked eye. **Microscopy** is the use of microscopes to view objects that cannot be seen with the unaided eye. The development of microscopes has been crucial for understanding cell biology.

Robert Hooke first observed cells in 1665 using an early microscope. Since then, microscope technology has advanced dramatically, allowing us to see increasingly fine details of cell structure.

## Key Concepts

### Magnification vs Resolution

**Magnification** is how much larger an image appears compared to the actual object.

$$\text{Magnification} = \frac{\text{Image size}}{\text{Actual size}}$$

**Resolution** is the ability to distinguish between two separate points that are close together. It's about the clarity and detail of the image.

- High magnification with low resolution = large, blurry image
- The best microscope has both high magnification AND high resolution

[DIAGRAM: Two images showing the difference between magnification and resolution]

### Types of Microscopes

#### 1. Light Microscopes (Optical Microscopes)

**How they work:**
- Use visible light and glass lenses to magnify
- Light passes through the specimen
- Lenses focus the light to create a magnified image

**Specifications:**
- Maximum useful magnification: ×1500
- Resolution: approximately 200 nm (0.2 μm)
- Can view living cells
- Specimens can be stained for better contrast

[DIAGRAM: Labelled diagram of a light microscope showing eyepiece lens, objective lenses, stage, mirror/light source, focus knobs]

**Parts of a Light Microscope:**

| Part | Function |
|------|----------|
| Eyepiece lens | Magnifies the image (usually ×10) |
| Objective lenses | Provide different magnifications (×4, ×10, ×40) |
| Stage | Platform where the slide is placed |
| Light source | Illuminates the specimen |
| Coarse focus | Rough focusing adjustment |
| Fine focus | Precise focusing adjustment |
| Condenser | Focuses light onto the specimen |

**Total Magnification:**
$$\text{Total magnification} = \text{Eyepiece magnification} \times \text{Objective magnification}$$

**Example:** Eyepiece ×10 and objective ×40 gives total magnification of ×400

#### 2. Electron Microscopes

Use a beam of electrons instead of light.

**Two Main Types:**

**Transmission Electron Microscope (TEM):**
- Electrons pass through a thin specimen
- Shows internal structures (like a slice through the cell)
- Maximum magnification: ×1,000,000
- Resolution: approximately 0.5 nm
- Specimens must be dead and very thin
- Images are 2D

**Scanning Electron Microscope (SEM):**
- Electrons bounce off the surface of the specimen
- Shows 3D surface structure
- Maximum magnification: ×500,000
- Resolution: approximately 3-10 nm
- Specimens must be dead
- Images show surface details

[DIAGRAM: Comparison of TEM and SEM images of the same cell]

### Comparison of Microscopes

| Feature | Light Microscope | TEM | SEM |
|---------|-----------------|-----|-----|
| Radiation used | Visible light | Electrons | Electrons |
| Max. magnification | ×1,500 | ×1,000,000 | ×500,000 |
| Resolution | 200 nm | 0.5 nm | 3-10 nm |
| Living specimens? | Yes | No | No |
| Colour? | Yes | No (false colour added) | No (false colour added) |
| Image type | 2D | 2D | 3D |
| Cost | Low | High | High |
| Specimen preparation | Simple | Complex | Complex |
| What you can see | Cells, nuclei, chloroplasts | Organelles, membranes | Surface detail |

### Using a Light Microscope

**Step-by-step procedure:**

1. **Place the slide** on the stage and secure with clips
2. **Start with lowest power** objective lens (×4)
3. **Use the coarse focus** to bring the specimen into rough focus
4. **Switch to higher power** objective (×10, then ×40)
5. **Use the fine focus** to sharpen the image
6. **Adjust the light** using the condenser or diaphragm

**Important tips:**
- Never use coarse focus with high power objectives (risk of breaking the slide)
- Always start with lowest magnification
- Keep both eyes open when using one eyepiece
- Clean lenses with lens paper only

### Preparing Slides

**Wet mount preparation:**
1. Place specimen on a clean glass slide
2. Add a drop of water or stain
3. Lower a cover slip at an angle to avoid air bubbles
4. Remove excess liquid with paper towel

**Common stains:**

| Stain | What it stains | Colour |
|-------|---------------|--------|
| Iodine | Starch, nuclei | Brown/blue-black |
| Methylene blue | Nuclei, cytoplasm | Blue |
| Eosin | Cytoplasm | Pink |
| Crystal violet | Bacteria | Purple |

[DIAGRAM: How to prepare a wet mount slide]

### Size Units in Microscopy

| Unit | Symbol | Relative size |
|------|--------|---------------|
| Metre | m | 1 m |
| Millimetre | mm | 0.001 m = 10⁻³ m |
| Micrometre | μm | 0.000001 m = 10⁻⁶ m |
| Nanometre | nm | 0.000000001 m = 10⁻⁹ m |

**Conversions:**
- 1 mm = 1000 μm
- 1 μm = 1000 nm
- 1 mm = 1,000,000 nm

**Typical sizes:**
- Animal cell: 10-100 μm
- Plant cell: 10-100 μm
- Bacterial cell: 1-5 μm
- Virus: 20-300 nm
- Ribosome: 20-30 nm

## Required Practical: Using a Microscope

**Aim:** To observe plant cells (e.g., onion epidermis) using a light microscope

**Method:**
1. Peel a thin layer of epidermis from an onion
2. Place on a slide with a drop of iodine solution
3. Add a cover slip carefully
4. Observe under low power first, then higher powers
5. Draw and label what you observe

**Expected observations:**
- Regular, rectangular cells
- Cell wall visible around each cell
- Nucleus stained dark by iodine
- Cytoplasm visible
- Large central vacuole (unstained)

## Common Exam Questions

- Calculate the total magnification of a microscope
- Compare light and electron microscopes
- Explain why electron microscopes have better resolution
- Describe how to prepare a slide for microscopy

## Common Misconceptions

- **Misconception:** Higher magnification always means better images
- **Reality:** Resolution is just as important. Without good resolution, higher magnification just makes a blurry image bigger

- **Misconception:** Electron microscopes show coloured images
- **Reality:** Electron microscopes produce black and white images. Colour is added artificially (false colour) to highlight structures

- **Misconception:** You can see individual atoms with any microscope
- **Reality:** Even electron microscopes cannot easily resolve individual atoms in biological specimens

## Practice Questions

1. State two differences between light and electron microscopes. (2 marks)

2. A microscope has an eyepiece lens of ×10 and an objective lens of ×40. Calculate the total magnification. (1 mark)

3. Explain the difference between magnification and resolution. (2 marks)

4. Describe how you would prepare a slide of onion cells for viewing under a light microscope. (4 marks)

5. A student wants to view the detailed internal structure of a mitochondrion. Explain which type of microscope they should use and why. (3 marks)

6. Explain why the development of electron microscopy significantly increased our understanding of cell structure. (6 marks)

## Key Terms Glossary

| Term | Definition |
|------|------------|
| Magnification | How many times larger an image is than the actual object |
| Resolution | Ability to distinguish between two points close together |
| Light microscope | Microscope using visible light and glass lenses |
| Electron microscope | Microscope using a beam of electrons |
| TEM | Transmission electron microscope - shows internal structure |
| SEM | Scanning electron microscope - shows surface detail |
| Objective lens | Lens closest to the specimen providing magnification |
| Eyepiece lens | Lens you look through, provides additional magnification |
| Stain | Dye used to make cell structures more visible |
| Micrometre (μm) | Unit of measurement = 10⁻⁶ metres |

## Summary

- Magnification is how much bigger an image is; resolution is the clarity/detail
- Light microscopes: max ×1500 magnification, 200 nm resolution, can view living cells
- Electron microscopes: much higher magnification and resolution, but specimens must be dead
- TEM shows internal structure; SEM shows 3D surface structure
- Total magnification = eyepiece magnification × objective magnification
- Unit conversions: 1 mm = 1000 μm = 1,000,000 nm
